item.text: {"text":"Recent work models histories as mixtures of persistent preferences and temporary interests. [HyperHawkes (WWW 2025)](https://evazangerle.at/publication/peintner-www-2025/) discovers latent intents through contrastive clustering, models recurring intent with Hawkes processes, and combines these signals with short-term attention mixtures. [Multi-interest sequential recommendation with contrastive learning and temporal analysis (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0950705124012917) groups similar items into interest subgraphs, models short-term interest changes, and separates interest representations through contrastive learning. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) separately encodes long- and short-term preferences using temporal embeddings and attention, then fuses them.\n\nRepetition versus exploration is another useful distinction: a [2026 Neural Networks framework](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026001838) combines gated attention denoising, partitioned repetition/exploration scoring, and an intent-discrimination margin loss. For this benchmark, a plausible adaptation is a small mixture of latent interests with candidate-dependent gates using elapsed time, recent interest concentration, and agreement between recent and historical representations. This is an implementation hypothesis, not an established result for these datasets. Because recommendations exclude seen items, transfer recurrence modeling to interests or related unseen items rather than copying consumed IDs. Observed transitions and title/description similarity can supply signals for related-item routing; they cannot establish that a purchase completed a purpose or that two products are complementary. Treat those interpretations as latent hypotheses and select adaptations using macro validation HR@10."}
